issues.legal_issue: Testimony given under oath before a committing court and admitted at trial as substantive evidence ordinarily requires extrinsic support when the witness gives a contradictory sworn account at trial, unless the factfinder is independently satisfied that the earlier account is true.
material_facts: A witness gave an account identifying the accused as participants in the killings before the committing court.
At the later trial, the witness gave a contradictory sworn account and said she had not seen the occurrence.
The earlier account was admitted as substantive evidence, but the record did not provide adequate extrinsic support for the witness's account of the occurrence and the accused's participation.
The court found unresolved difficulties in the earlier account, including uncertainty about the witness's opportunity to observe and unexplained aspects of the events.
issues.conclusion: The earlier testimony was substantive evidence and corroboration was not an absolute legal prerequisite. But in the ordinary case, it was unsafe to rely on it implicitly after the witness had made contradictory statements on oath; extrinsic support concerning both the occurrence and the particular accused's participation was ordinarily needed, unless the factfinder was independently satisfied of the truth of one account. On these facts, the testimony could not safely sustain the convictions without adequate corroboration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 288 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 made the committing-court testimony substantive evidence at trial, but did not make corroboration an absolute legal requirement. The Court relied on Bhuboni Sahu v. The King, A.I.R. 1949 P.C. 257, for the principle that it is unsafe to rely implicitly on a witness who has given two different stories on oath. Ordinarily, extrinsic evidence should reasonably support both the occurrence and the particular accused's participation; if the factfinder is independently satisfied of the truth of one statement despite the inconsistency, it may rely on it without such support.

rule.if: criminal_case and testimony_admitted_as_substantive_evidence and witness_gave_contradictory_sworn_accounts and not adequate_extrinsic_support and not factfinder_independently_satisfied

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the evidence is considered as a basis for conviction.
predicates.testimony_admitted_as_substantive_eviden: A witness's earlier testimony is admitted as substantive evidence in the later trial.
predicates.witness_gave_contradictory_sworn_account: The witness gave materially contradictory accounts under oath in different proceedings.
predicates.adequate_extrinsic_support: Evidence apart from the witness's disputed testimony reasonably supports both the occurrence and the particular accused's participation.
predicates.factfinder_independently_satisfied: The factfinder is independently satisfied, despite the contradictory sworn accounts, that one account is true.

issues.definition: When substantive testimony in a criminal case conflicts with the witness's other sworn account, it cannot safely support a conviction by itself if adequate outside support is absent and the factfinder is not independently satisfied of its truth.

issues.legal_issue: Blood traces on footwear do not provide sufficient corroboration of an accused's participation when the accused was taken to the bloodstained scene before the footwear was seized and the traces could have been acquired there.
material_facts: The witness's account was not independently adequate to support the convictions without corroboration.
Blood was found on the soles of footwear seized from two accused persons.
Before the footwear was seized, those accused had been brought to the scene, where the ground was bloodstained.
The blood traces could therefore have come from walking over the bloodstained ground, and no other sufficient corroboration of their participation was established.
issues.conclusion: The blood on the soles was not sufficient corroboration of the witness's account against those accused, so their convictions could not stand on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Applying the rule concerning contradictory sworn testimony and the need for ordinarily adequate extrinsic support, the Court held that evidence capable of an innocent explanation linked to the accused's prior presence at the scene did not sufficiently corroborate the witness's allegation of participation.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and disputed_witness_testimony_needs_corroboration and blood_found_on_footwear and accused_taken_to_bloodstained_scene_before_footwear_seized and scene_transfer_is_plausible and no_other_sufficient_corroboration

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.disputed_witness_testimony_needs_corrobo: The witness's disputed testimony cannot safely support the conviction without adequate corroboration.
predicates.blood_found_on_footwear: Blood was found on footwear associated with the accused.
predicates.accused_taken_to_bloodstained_scene_befo: The accused was taken to a scene with bloodstained ground before the footwear was seized.
predicates.scene_transfer_is_plausible: The blood on the footwear could plausibly have been acquired by walking over the bloodstained scene.
predicates.no_other_sufficient_corroboration: No other evidence sufficiently supported the allegation that the accused participated in the offence.

issues.definition: In an appeal against conviction, blood on footwear does not sufficiently corroborate disputed testimony when the accused had earlier been at a bloodstained scene, the traces could have come from that visit, and no other sufficient corroboration exists.
